questions.question: Selecting a reasonable switch platform for a large-scale Clos leaf role usually prioritizes:
options: High radix, predictable low latency, shallow-to-moderate buffers, and economics at massive port counts
Maximum deep buffer and chassis complexity on every ToR regardless of cost
Only enterprise campus PoE features
A single low-radix chassis for every rack
questions.explanation: Leaf: scale-out pizza-box / fixed form-factor ASICs; topology + ECMP absorb bursts.

questions.question: A deep-buffer or chassis platform is more justified when the role faces:
options: Bursty fan-in, speed mismatch, long-RTT/DCI, or aggregation where microbursts would drop on shallow silicon
Only idle lab traffic with perfect pacing
Wi-Fi access points exclusively
Situations where latency must always be minimized and bursts never occur
questions.explanation: Match buffer architecture to traffic reality—not prestige SKUs.

questions.question: A core large-scale design principle when choosing platforms is:
options: Fit silicon/form-factor to the tier’s job (leaf vs spine vs edge) under failure and growth assumptions—not one box for all roles
Always buy the most expensive chassis
Ignore oversubscription math
Optimize only for GUI cosmetics
questions.explanation: Design principles → platform selection.

questions.question: A pizza-box (fixed form-factor) switch is typically:
options: A self-contained 1–2RU system with onboard ASICs/ports—simple to deploy and replace at leaf scale
Always a multi-slot modular chassis with fabric cards
Only a server without networking
Unable to run L3
questions.explanation: Pizza-box = fixed box; chassis = modular slots.

questions.question: In a modular chassis, packet flow commonly involves:
options: Ingress line card → fabric/backplane → egress line card, with scheduling/VOQ credit systems to avoid fabric congestion
Only a single shared cable with no internal fabric
Packets skipping the chassis entirely
USB sneaker-net between cards
questions.explanation: Chassis packet path: linecard + fabric modules.

questions.question: Operational tradeoff of chassis vs pizza-box at hyperscale:
options: Chassis concentrate blast radius and complexity but can densify ports; pizza-boxes fail smaller and replace faster as a fleet
Chassis always have smaller blast radius
Pizza-boxes cannot be monitored
There is no operational difference
questions.explanation: Platform choice is also an ops/reliability choice.

questions.question: Life of a packet on a modern L3 leaf (simplified) is closest to:
options: Receive → parse/lookup (L2/L3/ACL) → buffer/schedule if needed → rewrite/TTL → transmit on chosen ECMP member
Only DNS then drop
Always software-forward on the CPU for every packet
Encrypt then ignore the FIB
questions.explanation: Pipeline literacy interviewers expect.

questions.question: Store-and-forward vs cut-through forwarding:
options: Store-and-forward buffers the frame (often with FCS check) before send; cut-through can start earlier for lower latency but with tradeoffs
Cut-through always validates the full FCS first
Store-and-forward never buffers
They are identical on all ASICs always
questions.explanation: Mode depends on speed mismatch, features, and congestion.

questions.question: Shallow-buffer switch ASICs typically:
options: Keep small fast on-chip buffers—low latency/high radix; rely on topology + endpoint congestion control for bursts
Hold seconds of every port in HBM by default
Eliminate the need for ECMP
Only work on the WAN edge
questions.explanation: Tomahawk/Trident-class shallow shared buffer model.

questions.question: Deep-buffer platforms primarily buy you:
options: Burst absorption (often with large off-chip memory / VOQ) at the cost of latency, power, and $/port
Always lower latency than shallow leaves
Infinite lossless behavior with zero congestion control
Free optics
questions.explanation: Jericho-class deep buffer tradeoff.

questions.question: Putting deep-buffer silicon on every short-reach compute leaf 'just in case' is often wrong because:
options: You pay latency/power/cost where a non-blocking Clos + shallow leaf + good congestion control is the intended design
Deep buffer always improves leaf latency
Shallow leaves cannot run BGP
Leaves never see microbursts of any kind
questions.explanation: Reasonable platform selection = role-appropriate.

questions.question: Incast (many-to-one fan-in) stresses shallow buffers because:
options: Many ingress flows simultaneously target one egress—queue builds faster than small on-chip buffers can absorb
Incast only affects DNS
Shallow buffers grow automatically to terabytes
ECMP removes all incast
questions.explanation: Classic DC congestion pattern; ECN/PFC/endpoint pacing matter.

questions.question: Virtual Output Queues (VOQ) in deep/chassis designs help by:
options: Queuing per destination so a congested egress less often head-of-line-blocks unrelated traffic across the fabric
Removing the need for any buffering
Only counting SNMP packets
Replacing routing protocols
questions.explanation: VOQ credit/scheduling is a chassis reliability/performance tool.

questions.question: Head-of-line blocking is a reliability/performance concern when:
options: A packet stuck for a congested destination delays other packets sharing the same queue/path resources
All queues are perfectly isolated forever
Only happens on Wi-Fi
It improves ECMP
questions.explanation: Why queue architecture and drop location matter.

questions.question: With shallow-buffer fabrics, ECN (and carefully designed PFC where used) matter because:
options: They signal or pause congestion before tiny buffers overflow—buffers alone are not the whole reliability story
They replace the need for capacity planning
PFC has no deadlock risk ever
ECN only works on dial-up
questions.explanation: Congestion control complements shallow silicon.

questions.question: An engineering mechanism that supports IP networking at scale is best exemplified by:
options: Standardized fabric designs, golden configs, automated validation, and intent/reconcile pipelines—not tribal CLI art
Unique snowflake configs per device with no review
Verbal-only change control
Disabling telemetry to save CPU
questions.explanation: JD: developing engineering mechanisms for IP systems at scale.

questions.question: A deployment mechanism for large-scale IP fabrics should include:
options: ZTP/turn-up checks, canary pools, health gates, and automatic stop/rollback on failed validation
Global unvalidated push on Friday night only
Manual USB per device with no inventory
Skipping optics/light-level checks
questions.explanation: JD: deployment mechanisms at scale.

questions.question: An operations mechanism that sustains IP networks at scale looks like:
options: Fleet-wide monitoring, runbooks, auto-remediation with guardrails, and COE-driven permanent fixes
Only paging random engineers without signals
Closing every Sev as 'user error'
No ownership of recurring flaps
questions.explanation: JD: operations mechanisms at scale.

questions.question: For a high-fan-in spine/aggregation facing mixed storage and speed mismatch, a reasonable platform signal is:
options: Evaluate deep-buffer/VOQ capability and sustained congestion behavior—not only port density marketing
Always the cheapest shallow leaf ASIC
Ignore buffer architecture entirely
Require Wi-Fi 7 support
questions.explanation: Spine/agg platform selection interview signal.

questions.question: 100G→10G (or similar) speed mismatch increases buffer pressure because:
options: Ingress can arrive faster than egress drains—queues build even without multi-flow incast
Lower speed always has infinite drain
Mismatch never causes drops
Only happens in chassis, never pizza-boxes
questions.explanation: NANOG ASIC talks: speed change is a classic buffer use case.

questions.question: High radix matters in fabric design because:
options: More ports per chip/box reduces tiers/hops and can simplify Clos scale-out—with power/buffer tradeoffs
Radix only means rack color
Lower radix always means fewer failures
Radix replaces routing
questions.explanation: Platform selection lever for large-scale environments.

questions.question: Choosing a feature-rich vs high-bandwidth/low-latency ASIC family is a design tradeoff about:
options: Needed features (ACL scale, tunneling, rich QoS) versus port speed/radix/buffer behavior for that tier
Always maximizing features on every leaf
Features never cost pipeline resources
Only the chassis color
questions.explanation: Reasonable platforms = fit-for-role silicon.

questions.question: As SDM Network Core, driving platform/mechanism excellence means:
options: Standards for which roles get which platform classes, plus software that makes deploy/operate safe at fleet scale
Letting every team pick random SKUs weekly
Banning all automation
Never documenting packet-flow assumptions
questions.explanation: People+tech leadership over platform strategy.

questions.question: Exception path to the control-plane CPU (punted packets) is a scale risk when:
options: Data-plane floods or soft faults punt too much traffic and melt the CPU/control plane
CPUs are infinitely fast for all packets
Punting always improves throughput
Only happens on pizza-boxes, never chassis
questions.explanation: Protect control plane; CoPP/rate-limit; keep forwarding in ASIC.
